paras: The attempted lynching of William Smith took place at Penryn Park, Pennsylvania, on the evening of July 13, 1888, when a crowd threatened to hang the older White Oak man just after his arrest on a charge of abducting five-year-old Bertha Beck. A man produced a rope and another struck Smith, but he was taken under guard to the jail at Lebanon. The Lancaster Intelligencer, which had called him a villain, soon rebuked the 'hotheads', and a Lebanon court acquitted Smith of the abduction in September.

Bertha Beck went missing from a Lancaster Sunday-school picnic at Penryn Park on Thursday, July 12, and searchers dragged the lake and fired dynamite in it without finding her. The next morning Smith, described as a 'charm worker' from nearby White Oak, came to the grounds with a 'magic glass' that he said could locate the child, and he spoke repeatedly of the reward.

About 6 p.m. Smith led two men down the railroad toward Mount Hope, and railroad men found the girl lying under brush near the stream below the lake. According to the Intelligencer, Smith tried to get away, was seized and was given into the charge of Special Officer Samuel Swenk, and the child then said he was the man who had taken her.

At the park station a 'very large and indignant crowd' surrounded him, there were threats of a 'necktie' party, and 'one hot-headed man procured a rope, which was not used'. One man struck Smith a heavy blow in the face, and at 6:30 Superintendent Neff of the railroad took him to Lebanon and placed him in jail. A later report said some men were angry enough to have lynched him had there not been a strong guard over the prisoner.

Smith's counsel waived a hearing at Lebanon on July 14, and on July 16 he gave $2,000 bail and went home to White Oak, where neighbors who believed him innocent met him. No arrest of anyone in the crowd is reported. At his trial in September, relatives and neighbors testified that he had been at home all day, and after the district attorney asked for acquittal the court acquitted him on September 20.

The Lancaster Daily Intelligencer covered the case almost alone, and its first full report treated Smith's guilt as settled, calling him 'the villain' and telling of the lynch talk without comment. Within days the paper changed its line: an editorial warned that the 'hotheads' at Penryn might have harmed 'a possibly innocent man', and another found 'small ground' for believing the girl had been taken by anyone. On July 18 it reprinted the Manheim Sun's interview with Smith, and out-of-state papers such as the Wilmington Daily Republican and the Camden Evening Telegram carried only brief wire items on the disappearance and the acquittal.

Smith gave a different account of the threat, saying that Jackson, the park superintendent, 'like a tiger started the cry' of 'lynch him! hang him!'. He also said that Neff 'had a rope and held me by the throat', while the Intelligencer described the rope holder only as an unnamed 'hot-headed man' and presented Neff as the official who took Smith to jail.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of William Smith at Penryn Park
bases: A crowd at the Penryn park station threatened to hang William Smith after his arrest on a charge of abducting a child, a man produced a rope and Smith was struck, but officers kept him and took him to jail (A3, A9, A10).

Smith was not killed: a large crowd threatened a 'necktie' party and a rope was procured, but the rope 'was not used' and he was taken to Lebanon jail under guard (A3, A9). It was a threatened lynching over an abduction accusation of which he was later acquitted (A12).

The Intelligencer's news report of the threat (A3), its follow-up and editorial (A4, A9) and Smith's own interview in the Manheim Sun (A10) agree that a crowd wanted to lynch him and that a rope appeared, though they differ on who held it.

accounts.label: Lancaster Intelligencer news report
accounts.gist: After his arrest Smith was surrounded at the park station by a large crowd; there were threats of a 'necktie' party, a man procured a rope that was not used, and one man struck Smith before Neff took him to Lebanon.

accounts.label: Smith's own account (Manheim Sun)
accounts.gist: Jackson 'like a tiger' started the cry 'lynch him! hang him!'; Neff had a rope and held him by the throat; Jackson was among the worst.

framing.detail: The first report called Smith 'the villain' and 'an old villain' who 'it has since been found caused' the disappearance, and told of the lynch talk under the headline 'TAKE [Talk] OF LYNCHING SMITH' without comment.
Two days later an Intelligencer editorial said the 'hotheads' at Penryn might have killed 'a possibly innocent man' and warned 'impulsive people' against hasty judgment.
Out-of-state papers carried only short wire items on the disappearance and the acquittal.

info: Friday, July 13, 1888, early evening, after the child was found about 6 p.m.; Smith was taken to Lebanon at 6:30
The railroad station at Penryn Park, a picnic resort on the Lebanon road near Mount Hope
William H. Smith of White Oak, Lancaster County, an old man (over 60) known as a 'charm worker'; race not stated
Accused of abducting Bertha Beck, 5, of Lancaster, from the Penryn Park picnic on July 12 and hiding her in the brush
A 'very large and indignant crowd' at the park station; Smith named Superintendent Jackson of the park as starting the cry and railroad superintendent Neff as the man with the rope
Smith was not lynched; he was jailed at Lebanon, waived a hearing, gave $2,000 bail and was released on Monday, July 16
